description:
In 2000, Enron was one of the most admired companies in America, worth around 70 billion dollars. Just over a year later, it was bankrupt. Its profits had been an illusion, and its own auditors were shredding documents.

This is the story of Enron: the energy company that turned into a Wall Street machine, the accounting trick that let it book profits that didn't exist, the journalist who asked one simple question, and the thousands of employees who lost everything.

• From pipelines to Wall Street stars
• Mark-to-market: profits from the future
• Andrew Fastow's secret companies
• One question from a journalist
• Shredded documents and the largest bankruptcy in US history

segments.text: In the summer of 2000, one company in Houston, Texas, was on top of the world. It was worth around 70 billion dollars. It reported about 100 billion dollars in revenue, one of the largest companies in America. Fortune magazine named it America's most innovative company six years in a row. Just over a year later, it was bankrupt, its shares were almost worthless, and its auditors were shredding documents. The company was Enron. And almost everything that made it look successful was an illusion.

Enron did not start as a Wall Street star. It was born in 1985 from the merger of two natural gas pipeline companies. Its boss was Ken Lay, a friendly, well connected economist who loved to talk about free markets. The business was simple and a bit boring: move natural gas through pipelines and get paid for it. But in the late eighties, the energy market in America was being deregulated, and Enron saw an opportunity to become something much more exciting.

That opportunity had a name: Jeff Skilling. Skilling was a brilliant consultant from McKinsey who joined Enron and transformed it. His idea was to treat energy like a financial product. Instead of just moving gas, Enron would buy and sell contracts for gas and electricity, like a bank trading stocks. Enron became a giant trading company. And to make that model look even better, Skilling asked for one special accounting rule.

The rule was called mark to market. Normally, a company records profit when it actually earns the money. With mark to market, Enron could sign a deal that would last, for example, twenty years, estimate all the profit it would make in the future, and record that profit today. Think about how dangerous that is. The profit was just an estimate, made by Enron itself. And if the deal failed later, the profit had already been reported.

Skilling was so happy when the rule was approved that, according to former employees, he celebrated with champagne. From then on, Enron had a machine to create impressive numbers. Every new deal could show a big profit on day one. The stock went up and up. Executives received huge bonuses tied to those numbers. And the pressure to keep finding new deals, and new profits, became enormous. But that was only the beginning of the trick.

Because some deals lost money. Some businesses, like a massive power plant in India and a broadband internet project, were disasters. Enron could not show those losses. So the chief financial officer, a young man called Andrew Fastow, created a network of hundreds of partnerships and special companies. Their names sounded like something from a movie: LJM, Chewco, Raptor. Their real purpose was to hide debt and losses off Enron's books.

Here is how it worked, in simple terms. Enron moved bad assets and debt into these outside companies, so they disappeared from Enron's own balance sheet. But many of these companies were secretly supported by Enron's own shares. As long as Enron's stock price kept going up, everything held together. If the stock fell, the whole structure would collapse. And Fastow himself was running some of these companies and earning tens of millions of dollars from them.

Meanwhile, Enron traders were making money in darker ways. During the California energy crisis of 2000 and 2001, the state suffered blackouts and electricity prices exploded. Later, recordings of Enron traders were released. In them, they joked about the high prices they were charging California and the money they were making. Investigations found that Enron had used trading strategies that helped manipulate the market. If you are enjoying this, subscribe, because this channel covers the biggest money stories in history.

Inside Enron, the culture made everything worse. The company used a brutal review system that employees nicknamed rank and yank. Every year, workers were ranked against each other, and those at the bottom, around fifteen percent, could be pushed out. So everybody wanted to bring in big deals with big numbers, fast. Nobody wanted to be the person who said a deal was bad. At the same time, a few short sellers on Wall Street, including an investor named Jim Chanos, started betting against Enron. They had read the reports carefully, and the numbers simply did not make sense.

The first crack came from a simple question. In March 2001, a journalist called Bethany McLean published an article in Fortune titled, more or less: is Enron overpriced? She asked something nobody on Wall Street was asking: how exactly does Enron make its money? The company's financial reports were so complicated that even professional analysts could not explain them. Enron's executives reacted angrily. But the question was out.

In February 2001, Jeff Skilling had finally become CEO. Just six months later, in August, he suddenly resigned, saying it was for personal reasons. Ken Lay came back to run the company and told employees that Enron's stock was a great buy. At the same time, a vice president called Sherron Watkins wrote to Lay warning him that the company might implode in a wave of accounting scandals. The storm was coming.

In October 2001, Enron announced a big quarterly loss and a huge reduction in its shareholders' equity, over a billion dollars, linked to Fastow's partnerships. The market panicked. Weeks later, Enron admitted it had overstated its profits for years, going back to 1997. A rival company, Dynegy, tried to buy Enron and save it, but pulled out. The stock, which had been around 90 dollars at its peak, fell below one dollar.

On December 2nd, 2001, Enron filed for bankruptcy. It was the largest bankruptcy in American history at the time. And then the story got even worse. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, one of the five biggest accounting firms in the world, had been shredding Enron documents. Andersen was convicted of obstruction of justice in 2002. The Supreme Court later overturned that conviction, but it was too late. The firm had already collapsed, and tens of thousands of people lost their jobs.

The real victims were the employees. Around 20,000 people lost their jobs. Many of them had their retirement savings invested in Enron stock, because the company encouraged it. When the stock collapsed, their savings collapsed with it, while the rules temporarily stopped many of them from selling. Meanwhile, some top executives had sold shares worth hundreds of millions of dollars before the fall.

Justice came, but slowly. Andrew Fastow pleaded guilty and served around six years in prison. Jeff Skilling was convicted in 2006 and sentenced to 24 years, later reduced. He was released in 2019. Ken Lay was also convicted in 2006, but he died of a heart attack a few weeks later, before he was sentenced. And in 2002, the United States passed a new law, the Sarbanes Oxley Act, to force companies to be more honest about their accounts.

So what is the lesson of Enron? The first one is simple: if nobody can explain how a company makes money, that is a warning sign, not a sign of genius. The second one is darker. Enron's employees had a code of ethics that was more than sixty pages long. The company's slogan was ask why. And yet almost nobody asked why until it was too late.

Enron was not destroyed by a single lie. It was destroyed by a system where everybody benefited as long as the numbers went up: executives, bankers, auditors and even many investors. When the numbers were fake, nobody wanted to be the one to say it. Tell me in the comments: do you think a scandal like Enron could happen again today? Or is it already happening somewhere?

segments.text: In 2000, Enron was worth around 70 billion dollars and was called America's most innovative company. The secret? An accounting rule that let it record profits from deals that would take twenty years to pay. Losses were hidden in hundreds of secret companies with names like Raptor. One journalist asked a simple question: how does Enron actually make money? A year later, it was bankrupt, and its auditors were shredding documents. The full story is on the channel.
